# Can a 500,000-Passenger Airport Change Its Region? Evidence, Magnitudes, and Causal Limits

Yes—conditionally. An airport handling about 500,000 annual passenger movements can generate measurable employment, wages, output, tourism spending, tax revenue, and connectivity benefits in its surrounding economy. Near-threshold examples include Prince George Airport at 506,486 passengers in 2018, Norwich Airport at 453,000 passengers in the year ending March 2026, Cornwall Airport Newquay at 400,311 reported passengers in financial year 2024/25, and Tri-Cities Airport in Tennessee at 448,514 passengers in 2023. Their reported effects range from hundreds of airport-related jobs to regional GVA estimates of approximately £100–184 million, although several claims do not disclose enough methodological detail to establish causation.[Prince George Airport traffic profile](https://www.pgairport.ca/yxs-passenger-numbers-hit-the-half-million-mark/)[Norwich Airport passenger and economic-impact announcement](https://www.norwichairport.co.uk/norwich-airports-continued-growth-sees-annual-passenger-numbers-up-5/)[Cornwall Airport Newquay Sustainability Report](https://www.cornwallairportnewquay.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/CAN-Sustainability-Report-2024-25.pdf)[Tri-Cities Airport passenger announcement](https://flytri.com/tri-cities-airport-reports-impressive-surge-in-passenger-numbers-for-2023/)

The strongest quantity aligned with 500,000 total passengers is a 2024 Canadian airport-system estimate. Its simple proportional translation associates 500,000 total passengers with approximately 745 direct jobs, $58 million in wages, $87 million in GDP, $214.5 million in economic output, and $29 million in direct taxes. Those are model-based averages, not an observed airport at exactly 500,000 passengers, not a causal estimate, and not a confidence interval.[Canadian Airports Council economic-impact study](https://canadasairports.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/ACI-NA-Econ-Canada-Report-20250425.pdf)

The evidence therefore supports the proposition that an airport at this scale can have significant and measurable socioeconomic effects. It does not show that 500,000 passengers is a universal threshold, that passenger volume alone causes the effects, or that the net regional welfare after subsidies, capital costs, leakage, displacement, and environmental or congestion costs is necessarily positive. The appropriate overall verdict is conditional support.

The report first defines the passenger exposure, region, and meaning of “significant.” It then identifies comparable near-threshold airports, presents measured outcomes and transmission mechanisms, examines causal designs and counterexamples, compares effect magnitudes on common but carefully qualified measures, assesses data limitations and heterogeneity, and ends with a threshold-specific verdict.

## 1. Hypothesis, definitions, and decision rule

### What exactly is the hypothesis?

The hypothesis tested here is:

> An airport handling 500,000 passengers per year can generate significant and measurable socioeconomic impacts in its surrounding region.

The verb “can” matters. It is an existential claim about possibility, not a claim that every airport with that throughput will have the same effect. A stronger proposition would be that every 500,000-passenger airport produces a large net regional benefit because of passenger volume alone. The evidence does not support that stronger proposition.

The exposure also needs to be specified. In airport statistics, “passengers” can mean several different things:

- total passenger throughput, often the sum of enplaned and deplaned passengers;
- enplanements, meaning passengers boarding aircraft;
- deplanements, meaning passengers arriving from aircraft;
- arrivals plus departures, sometimes with connecting passengers counted in the airport’s published series;
- scheduled passenger seats; or
- unique people, a measure rarely used in airport traffic reporting.

The Federal Aviation Administration defines passenger boarding as enplanement data extracted from its Air Carrier Activity database. It uses full-calendar-year enplanements to classify airports and allocate funds, so FAA enplanements are not the same exposure as total arrivals plus departures.[FAA passenger-boarding statistics](https://www.faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/passenger_allcargo_stats/passenger) The U.S. Bureau of Transportation Statistics likewise reports scheduled enplaned revenue passengers and separate arrival and departure fields in its airport data.[BTS airport data](https://www.transtats.bts.gov/airports.asp)

For this review, the principal interpretation of 500,000 is 500,000 total annual passenger movements—an airport’s combined passenger throughput rather than 500,000 additional boardings. That is the interpretation most closely matched by the Canadian Airports Council’s “1 million total passengers” relationship. Where a source uses enplanements, departing seats, or an undefined “PAX” field, the result is kept separate rather than silently converted.

A total passenger count is not a count of unique residents or visitors. A person flying out and later returning may appear once as an enplanement and once as a deplanement. Connecting passengers may be counted differently from origin-and-destination passengers. These distinctions matter because local economic effects depend more on where passengers spend money, work, and conduct business than on how many times a passenger record appears in a traffic total.

### What counts as significant?

There is no supplied study that establishes a universal statistical or practical threshold for calling an airport impact “significant.” The 2019 Norfolk International Airport study defines economic impact through employment, earnings, GDP, and output but does not set a formal percentage or statistical cutoff.[Norfolk International Airport economic-impact study](http://www.flyorf.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/ORF-Economic-Impact-2019-FINAL-REPORT-22Jul2020.pdf)

This review therefore uses two distinct meanings:

1. **Practical significance:** the effect is large enough to be economically consequential or visible in regional accounts—for example, hundreds of jobs, tens of millions of dollars in wages or GVA, measurable visitor spending, tax revenue, or a material change in connectivity.

2. **Statistical significance:** the estimated airport effect is distinguishable from zero under a defined statistical model, comparison group, and uncertainty measure such as a confidence interval or p-value.

A result can be practically large but causally weak. An input-output model may calculate hundreds of jobs and millions of dollars of output without demonstrating that the airport created those activities rather than attracting them from another location. Conversely, a statistically precise estimate can be economically modest. The two standards must not be conflated.

The primary decision rule is therefore:

- support the hypothesis if near-threshold or transferable evidence shows measurable regional outcomes and the mechanisms are plausible;
- qualify the conclusion according to the exposure definition, geographic denominator, and identification method; and
- withhold a universal or causal threshold claim when the evidence lacks a same-year 500,000-passenger observation, a comparison region, or a net-benefit calculation.

### What is the surrounding region?

“Surrounding region” is not a fixed geographic unit. Airport effects occur at several spatial levels:

- **airport site:** airport employees, tenants, airlines, ground handlers, security, concessions, maintenance, and public agencies;
- **near-airport area:** hotels, rental-car firms, logistics companies, suppliers, and businesses that benefit from airport access;
- **local catchment:** the city and communities whose residents use the airport;
- **administrative or economic region:** a county, metropolitan area, province, state, or wider economic catchment;
- **network region:** the wider area affected by connectivity, tourism, investment, labor mobility, or cargo flows.

The geographic boundary changes the measured result. A wider region captures more supplier purchases and household spending before money leaks outside the study area, but it can also include economic activity that would not otherwise be attributed to the airport. A narrow local boundary may better represent local benefit but exclude legitimate spillovers.

The Hamilton airport study illustrates the issue. It defines the local geography as the Hamilton Census Metropolitan Area and the wider geography as Ontario. About half of the airport-related impact was estimated to leak from Hamilton to the rest of Ontario. The Hamilton multiplier for industry activity was 1.37, while the Ontario multiplier was 2.36 because the larger economy retained more rounds of indirect and induced spending.[Hamilton International Airport economic-impact analysis](https://flyhamilton.ca/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/HamiltonAirportEIAReport_FinalSubmitted.pdf)

Other studies use different boundaries. The Palomar study covers five counties in the San Diego region and separately identifies North County and Carlsbad. The Dane County Regional Airport study covers Dane County plus seven neighboring counties. The Gerald R. Ford study reports both Kent County and a 13-county West Michigan region. A Brazilian airport methodology uses municipalities within a 200-kilometer radius, while Volkhausen’s European study uses NUTS-3 regions and a 25-kilometer airport buffer.[Palomar Airport economic-impact analysis](https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/dam/sdc/dpw/AIRPORTS/palomar/documents/Master-Plan-Update/2021/Palomar_Airport_Economic_Impact_Analysis-9.28.21.pdf)[Dane County Regional Airport study](https://msnairport.com/documents/pdf/DCRA-Economic-Impact-Study-Report-021626.pdf)[Future Transportation airport methodology](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-7590/3/3/62)[Volkhausen regional-airport study](https://www.wiserpub.com/uploads/1/20220809/a34784bc2e82b267978ff56b9963ee42.pdf)

The meaningful definition for this report is therefore the source’s declared local or economic catchment, not an assumed universal radius. Results from different geographies are compared only after stating what each denominator captures.

### Why baseline and additional passengers must be separated

An airport’s total annual impact is not the same as the impact of adding passengers to an existing airport. A baseline estimate includes fixed and semi-fixed operations, existing tenants, routes, facilities, and regional business relationships. A marginal estimate asks what changes when activity rises by a relatively small amount.

The National Academies explicitly warns that marginal airport estimates should not be substituted for average total impacts. Average jobs per passenger calculated from an airport’s total reported impact may overstate the effect of an additional passenger, while a marginal estimate may understate the airport’s full contribution when fixed activities are important.[National Academies discussion of airport economic impacts](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5)

The distinction is central to the threshold question. “500,000 total passengers” describes a baseline scale. “500,000 additional enplanements” describes a very large increment to an existing airport. The two quantities cannot be treated as interchangeable.

### The decision rule for this review

The evidence will be considered supportive when it establishes at least one of the following:

- an airport near 500,000 passengers reports measurable direct or regional outcomes;
- a system-wide model aligned with total passenger throughput provides a conditional magnitude;
- a credible causal study finds airport activity affects regional employment, income, GDP, business activity, tourism, or property values; or
- a connectivity or route mechanism plausibly transmits airport activity into regional productivity or investment.

It will be considered insufficient for a universal threshold claim when it lacks:

- a standardized passenger definition;
- same-year traffic and impact data;
- a declared geographic denominator;
- a comparison region or counterfactual;
- confidence intervals or other uncertainty measures; or
- accounting for public costs, displacement, leakage, and traffic diverted from other airports.

This approach allows the underlying analysis to continue even where an exact aggregate statistic is unavailable. It also prevents a modeled gross contribution from being presented as a causal net benefit.
