The table provides evidence of measurable activity close to the proposed scale, but it is not a standardized treatment sample. YXS has the best alignment with total passenger throughput because its 2018 release explicitly describes arrivals, departures, and connections. Norwich, Newquay, and TRI use airport-reported passenger labels without a fully documented directional definition. PSC uses enplanements, while Hamilton combines passenger and cargo operations.

### Prince George: the closest explicitly defined throughput case

Prince George Airport crossed 500,000 in 2018 with 506,486 passengers. The airport’s published series identifies the measure as including arrivals, departures, and connections, making it the closest available exposure to the review’s principal definition. Its passenger count had risen from 339,858 in 2003 to 506,486 in 2018, alongside terminal, baggage, international-arrivals, runway, and cargo-warehouse investments.[YXS 2018 traffic profile](https://www.pgairport.ca/yxs-passenger-numbers-hit-the-half-million-mark/)

The later master plan uses a different formulation. It describes activity as enplaned/deplaned passengers and reports a high between 497,000 and 506,000 passengers between 2017 and 2019. It also reports six passenger carriers, two dedicated cargo carriers, nine fixed- and rotary-wing operators, and 13 supporting organizations. The airport therefore represents more than a passenger terminal: its regional role includes cargo, air ambulance, wildfire suppression, resource-sector charters, flight training, business aviation, and recreational aviation.[YXS master plan](https://www.pgairport.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/PGAA_2023_Master_Plan_Update-Final_Report-2023_04_13_Compressed.pdf)

Recent traffic shows why a single threshold year should not be treated as a permanent airport condition. The airport’s year-in-review series lists 496,714 passengers in 2019, 176,994 in 2020, 201,506 in 2021, 364,663 in 2022, 417,848 in 2023, and 450,494 in 2024. The 2025 release reports 443,366 passengers, 1.6% below 2024, while seat capacity rose 6%.[YXS 2024 year-in-review](https://www.pgairport.ca/2024-passenger-numbers-and-year-in-review/)[YXS 2025 traffic release](https://www.pgairport.ca/prince-george-airport-reports-stable-passenger-volumes/)

The master plan’s introductory discussion gives a somewhat different 2019 figure of 474,500 and a 2020 figure of 161,500. These discrepancies do not invalidate the general scale, but they show why traffic definitions and source series must be preserved rather than merged into a synthetic time series.

### Norwich: a connectivity- and resource-sector case

Norwich Airport reported 453,000 passengers in the year ending 31 March 2026, a 5% increase. Its route inventory—16 direct destinations in nine countries and access to more than 160 destinations through Amsterdam—gives the passenger count a connectivity dimension that a bare throughput statistic cannot capture.[Norwich Airport 2026 announcement](https://www.norwichairport.co.uk/norwich-airports-continued-growth-sees-annual-passenger-numbers-up-5/)

Norwich also reported a 3,000-passenger increase in helicopter traffic and described itself as a gateway to the southern North Sea offshore-energy industry. This matters because the same passenger total can support very different regional effects depending on whether traffic is primarily leisure travel, local residents connecting through a hub, offshore workers, business travelers, or visitors spending money in the region.

The reported £184 million GVA and 2,840 local jobs are therefore relevant evidence that an airport near the proposed threshold can be associated with a sizeable regional footprint. They are not, however, a threshold-specific causal estimate. The supplied announcement does not identify the study’s year, GVA accounting boundary, treatment of induced effects, counterfactual, or confidence interval.

### Newquay: tourism and local-supply-chain channels

Cornwall Airport Newquay reports 400,311 PAX in financial year 2024/25. The airport’s sustainability report does not define PAX, so the number cannot be assumed to be arrivals plus departures. The same report says the airport creates approximately £100 million in annual GVA for Cornwall through employment, tourism, and business connectivity.[Cornwall Airport Newquay Sustainability Report](https://www.cornwallairportnewquay.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/CAN-Sustainability-Report-2024-25.pdf)

The report also identifies a local-procurement mechanism. It says the airport works with 38 café and retail businesses and that 92% of its suppliers are local. Those figures indicate a channel through which airport spending may reach local firms, but they do not reveal supplier expenditure, local employment, or the definition of “local.”

Newquay’s earlier recovery provides a warning about temporal inference. BBC News reported more than 250,000 passengers in 2022, up by 150,000 from 2021, with airport managers forecasting 450,000 passengers in 2023. The airport had closed in early 2020, reopened in July, closed again in November because of weak demand, and reopened later in 2021. The subsequent passenger increase therefore cannot be treated as a clean airport-caused change in Cornwall’s economy.[BBC News on Newquay traffic and closures](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-cornwall-65103131)

### TRI and PSC: two different Tri-Cities airports

The name Tri-Cities Airport refers to two different cases and must not be conflated.

TRI, in Northeast Tennessee, reported 448,514 total passengers in 2023. It serves a broad multi-state area and offers nonstop flights to five hubs. Its 2021–2023 traffic pattern shows a strong recovery from pandemic disruption, but no supplied study reports its regional employment, GDP, tourism, tax, or investment effects.[TRI 2023 traffic announcement](https://flytri.com/tri-cities-airport-reports-impressive-surge-in-passenger-numbers-for-2023/)

PSC, in Pasco, Washington, is a different airport. Its 2018 traffic measure is 395,348 scheduled enplanements, not total arrivals plus departures. It also had 30,000 general-aviation operations and a broad aviation ecosystem including cargo, agricultural spraying, aircraft sales and rental, flight training, and emergency services.[WSDOT PSC profile](https://wsdot.wa.gov/publications/fulltext/aviation/PSC-TriCities.pdf)

PSC is useful because WSDOT provides a detailed airport-level impact model. It is less useful as a pure passenger-throughput case because the model includes activities that do not scale simply with scheduled passenger boardings.

### Hamilton: a near-threshold but cargo-heavy comparator

Hamilton International Airport handled nearly 600,000 passengers in 2017, making it a useful comparator near the upper edge of the requested scale. Its regional role, however, is heavily shaped by cargo. The airport handled approximately 98,000 tonnes of cargo and about 500 million kilograms of aircraft billable weight. Cargojet used it as a primary hub, while UPS and DHL operated scheduled cross-border freight services.[Hamilton economic-impact analysis](https://flyhamilton.ca/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/HamiltonAirportEIAReport_FinalSubmitted.pdf)

ICF estimated 3,450 jobs, $243.5 million in labor income, $385.7 million in value added, and approximately $1.2 billion in Hamilton industry activity. Passenger operations accounted for 250 direct badged employees and approximately 380 total modeled jobs. Cargo operations accounted for approximately 1,710 modeled jobs in the detailed table. This is evidence that an airport near 500,000–600,000 passengers can have substantial regional effects, but it also demonstrates why passenger count alone is an inadequate exposure measure.

## 3. Measured regional socioeconomic outcomes

### Direct airport activity

Direct effects are the first economic transactions associated with airport operations. They include airport management, airlines, ground handling, security, maintenance, government agencies, rental cars, concessions, construction, and other tenants. They may also include spending by non-local visitors after they arrive, depending on the study.

The Canadian Airports Council’s 2024 study reports 224,500 direct jobs across 61 airports, with $17.5 billion in direct wages, $26.2 billion in direct GDP, and $64.7 billion in direct output. It combines published impact studies for 33 airports with regression estimates for 28 smaller airports.[Canadian Airports Council study](https://canadasairports.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/ACI-NA-Econ-Canada-Report-20250425.pdf)

The Prince George evidence shows how direct activity can extend beyond passenger processing. Its 2018 profile reports more than 28 airport businesses with over 200 employees. The 2023 master plan identifies carriers, cargo firms, helicopter operators, air ambulance services, wildfire operations, flight training, maintenance, fuel, security, catering, and air-traffic services. These activities create direct employment even when they are weakly related to the passenger count.

Prince George’s airport authority reports that the airport supported 770 person-years of employment and $24 million in wages in 2011, and generated $106 million in economic activity. The source does not disclose whether the $106 million is output, GDP, or another measure, nor does it provide a control region. The result is therefore a measured airport contribution, not a causal estimate.[Prince George Airport economic-impact page](https://www.pgairport.ca/business-information/air-service-development/)

Norwich reports approximately 250 direct employees within its larger estimate of 2,840 local jobs. The gap between direct and total jobs is consistent with a direct-to-regional transmission mechanism involving suppliers, visitor spending, and sector-specific activity, but the supplied material does not show how much of the gap is indirect, induced, visitor-related, or catalytic.

PSC provides the clearest near-threshold decomposition. WSDOT estimates 659 jobs from on-airport activity and 808 jobs from visitor spending, for 1,467 direct jobs. It then estimates 300 supplier-sales jobs and 427 jobs from worker-income re-spending, producing 2,194 total jobs. The corresponding total measures are $99.128 million in labor income, $173.516 million in value added, and $290.603 million in business revenues.[WSDOT PSC economic-impact profile](https://wsdot.wa.gov/publications/fulltext/aviation/PSC-TriCities.pdf)

These figures are not all the same type of quantity. Jobs, labor income, value added, and business revenues are separate dimensions and should not be added together. The WSDOT report also states that the metrics represent different components of airport impact and are not additive across dimensions.

### Indirect and induced activity

Indirect effects arise when airport businesses purchase goods and services from suppliers. Induced effects arise when employees spend wages in the regional economy. Input-output models calculate successive rounds of such spending until money leaks outside the geographic boundary through imports, savings, taxes, or purchases from firms elsewhere.

The Canadian study reports 211,300 multiplier jobs in addition to 224,500 direct jobs. Multiplier effects account for $15.4 billion in wages, $23.4 billion in GDP, and $58.8 billion in output. The national totals are therefore 435,800 jobs, $32.9 billion in wages, $49.6 billion in GDP, and $123.5 billion in output.[Canadian Airports Council study](https://canadasairports.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/ACI-NA-Econ-Canada-Report-20250425.pdf)

PSC’s decomposition is similar in structure: 300 supplier-sales jobs and 427 worker-income re-spending jobs beyond 1,467 direct jobs. Hamilton’s IMPLAN model separates 2,300 direct jobs from 180 indirect jobs and 950 induced jobs within Hamilton. The Hamilton study reports a 1.37 total industry-activity multiplier for the Hamilton CMA and a 2.36 multiplier for Ontario, illustrating the effect of geographic leakage.[Hamilton economic-impact analysis](https://flyhamilton.ca/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/HamiltonAirportEIAReport_FinalSubmitted.pdf)

The Australian evidence provides a threshold-adjacent estimate for smaller regional airports. ACIL Allen estimated that all Australian regional airports with fewer than 500,000 annual passenger movements spent approximately $185.4 million in 2014/15 and induced an additional $83.4 million in spending elsewhere in the Australian economy. It estimated approximately 1,720 airport FTEs across the group and 2,750 additional FTEs in the rest of the Australian economy. For a typical RPT regional airport, the estimated induced spending was approximately $830,000 per year.[ACIL Allen regional-airport analysis](https://treasury.gov.au/sites/default/files/2019-03/360985-Australian-Airports-Association-supporting-documents.pdf)

That evidence supports the existence of measurable supplier and induced channels below the threshold. It does not establish the impact of one airport at exactly 500,000 movements, because the figures aggregate many airports and use fitted relationships and previously estimated coefficients.

### Tourism and visitor spending

Visitor spending is potentially one of the largest channels because it can bring new money into the region. Visitors may spend on accommodation, food and beverages, local transportation, entertainment, recreation, and retail. The Transportation Research Board recommends identifying airport visitors, estimating spending by visitor type and category, adjusting retail spending for the local share, and applying industry employment and wage data.[TRB visitor-spending framework](https://crp.trb.org/acrpwebresource1/visitor-spending/)

The effect depends on whether passengers are inbound visitors, local residents traveling outward, or transfer passengers. Spending by an inbound visitor may be new money to the region. Spending by a resident who would otherwise depart from another airport may represent a change in airport choice rather than new regional demand. A transfer passenger may generate little local spending.

Norwich’s direct destinations and Amsterdam connectivity provide access to tourism and business markets, while Newquay explicitly identifies tourism as one of the channels behind its reported GVA. The Newquay report’s 38 terminal businesses and 92% local-supplier share indicate local commercial activity, but they do not quantify visitor spending or distinguish inbound tourism from local outbound travel.[Cornwall Airport Newquay Sustainability Report](https://www.cornwallairportnewquay.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/CAN-Sustainability-Report-2024-25.pdf)

Larger airports provide more complete examples. In 2019, more than 900,000 visitors arriving through Norfolk International Airport were estimated to spend more than $620 million in Virginia. The report attributes that visitor spending to 8,460 direct jobs and 11,120 jobs after indirect and induced effects, with $603 million in GDP in the total visitor category.[Norfolk International Airport economic-impact study](http://www.flyorf.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/ORF-Economic-Impact-2019-FINAL-REPORT-22Jul2020.pdf)

Dane County Regional Airport handled 2,347,990 total passengers in 2024. Tourism Economics estimated $128.4 million in direct off-airport visitor spending and $203.2 million in total visitor-related business sales, supporting 1,366 total visitor-related jobs in its eight-county study region.[Dane County Regional Airport study](https://msnairport.com/documents/pdf/DCRA-Economic-Impact-Study-Report-021626.pdf)

These larger cases demonstrate the mechanism but cannot be scaled mechanically to 500,000 passengers. Visitor shares, length of stay, hotel capacity, attractions, route mix, and the proportion of non-local passengers may differ sharply.

### Wages, household income, GDP, GVA, and output

Several near-threshold cases report monetary outcomes:

- Norwich reports approximately £184 million in regional GVA and 2,840 local jobs at 453,000 passengers.
- Newquay reports approximately £100 million in annual Cornwall GVA at 400,311 reported PAX.
- PSC reports $173.516 million in modeled value added at 395,348 scheduled enplanements, together with $99.128 million labor income.
- Prince George reports $24 million in wages and 770 person-years in 2011, at a traffic level that was below or near the later threshold.
- Hamilton reports $385.7 million in modeled value added and $243.5 million in labor income at nearly 600,000 passengers, but cargo is a dominant component.
- The Canadian system average translates to $87 million in direct GDP and $58 million in direct wages for 500,000 total passengers under a simple proportional calculation.

The figures are not directly interchangeable. GVA and GDP are value-added measures; industry activity and business revenues include gross transactions and may contain intermediate purchases; wages and labor income may include benefits and proprietor income; and jobs may be FTEs, person-years, or counts of employees.

Palomar illustrates both the value of wage information and the importance of the denominator. Its 2019 baseline estimates 2,594 jobs, $168.1 million in labor income, $460.6 million in industry activity, and $72.2 million in tax revenue across a five-county San Diego region. Air-transportation occupations averaged $74,972 in annual compensation, compared with $66,698 across North County. The compensation comparison is measurable but does not establish that the airport caused a regional wage premium.[Palomar Airport economic-impact analysis](https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/dam/sdc/dpw/AIRPORTS/palomar/documents/Master-Plan-Update/2021/Palomar_Airport_Economic_Impact_Analysis-9.28.21.pdf)

Prince George provides a cautious regional-scale illustration. Its 2021 economic profile reports 43,810 employed residents and $5.7 billion in household and business income.[Prince George economic profile](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/campaigns/immigration-matters/local-economies/prince-george.html) If the Canadian system-average estimate of 745 direct jobs and $87 million in GDP were mechanically applied to a region with those characteristics, the jobs would equal approximately 1.7% of employed residents and the GDP proxy would equal approximately 1.5% of reported income. This is not an estimate of YXS’s actual regional effect, and income is not GDP; it merely shows why hundreds of jobs or tens of millions of dollars can be practically important in a small regional economy.

### Business activity, investment, and productivity

Airport connectivity can affect regional economic performance through channels that input-output models often omit. These include:

- access to suppliers and customers;
- business travel and face-to-face contact;
- recruitment and retention of specialized labor;
- tourism and convention markets;
- time-sensitive cargo;
- foreign investment;
- innovation and knowledge transfer;
- land development around the airport; and
- resilience during emergencies or resource-sector projects.

The Prince George master plan describes the airport as supporting forestry, mining, energy, construction, transportation, professional services, medical travel, wildfire suppression, and emergency services. It also identifies a possible logistics and e-commerce role, although it states that current air cargo is modest and most regional freight moves by road and rail.[YXS master plan](https://www.pgairport.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/PGAA_2023_Master_Plan_Update-Final_Report-2023_04_13_Compressed.pdf)

The Hamilton study provides a concrete example of a cargo-driven productivity channel. Its cargo operations support pharmaceutical, medical-device, perishables, automotive, aerospace, and e-commerce supply chains. The airport also hosts maintenance, repair, and overhaul activity and aerospace training. Those benefits arise from the airport’s schedule, cargo facilities, operating hours, and industrial relationships, not merely from the passenger count.

The Transportation Research Board’s case-study synthesis reports increasing foreign investment and job growth in regions served by airports with international service, particularly Austin, San Diego, and Raleigh-Durham after new European nonstop routes. But it does not provide a threshold-specific effect size or a controlled estimate.[TRB airport and regional-economic-activity synthesis](https://crp.trb.org/acrpwebresource12/measuring-air-service-and-regional-economic-activity/general-observations-of-the-case-studies/)

Bilotkach’s dynamic-panel study of U.S. metropolitan areas provides stronger evidence that connectivity matters. Using a generalized method-of-moments estimator, it finds that the number of nonstop destinations has a clearer and more robust association with regional employment, business establishments, and average wages than passenger-traffic volume alone. At the sample median, an additional destination is associated with 98 jobs and four new business establishments; at the sample mean, the corresponding figures are 223 jobs and 15 establishments.[Bilotkach airport-connectivity study](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0042098015576869)

The result is directly relevant to the threshold hypothesis: 500,000 passengers routed through a few weakly connected destinations may have less regional effect than a similar passenger total supporting a diverse network of direct and hub connections. Passenger volume is therefore an incomplete measure of the airport’s economic function.

### Tax revenue and property values

Tax revenue is measurable in several studies, but it is usually reported as gross tax generation rather than net fiscal benefit after public expenditure.

PSC’s 2018 model estimates $1.7167 million in local county and municipal taxes, $9.91116 million in Washington State taxes, and $11.62786 million in total taxes. The total includes taxes associated with on-airport activity and visitor spending.[WSDOT PSC profile](https://wsdot.wa.gov/publications/fulltext/aviation/PSC-TriCities.pdf)

The Canadian system model estimates $58 million in direct taxes per 1 million total passengers. A simple proportional calculation therefore gives approximately $29 million in direct taxes for 500,000 total passengers. As with the employment and GDP figures, this is a system-average model output, not an observed airport-level fiscal result.

At larger airports, tax values are much higher. Norfolk’s 2019 report estimates more than $300 million in annual taxes from operations, capital improvements, and visitor spending. Dane County Regional Airport’s 2024 study estimates $491.2 million in total taxes across its eight-county region, including $337.7 million in state and local taxes.[Norfolk International Airport economic-impact study](http://www.flyorf.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/ORF-Economic-Impact-2019-FINAL-REPORT-22Jul2020.pdf)[Dane County Regional Airport study](https://msnairport.com/documents/pdf/DCRA-Economic-Impact-Study-Report-021626.pdf)

Property values can move in either direction. Airport access and connectivity may increase values for some commercial or residential locations, while aircraft noise, traffic, safety concerns, and land-use restrictions may reduce them. The supplied property studies are not near-threshold airport cases, but they demonstrate the mixed pattern:

- A Manchester study found prices 6.09% lower in many noise-affected postcodes, but the effect disappeared after neighborhood controls.
- A difference-in-differences study of Hong Kong airport relocation found a 24.43% relative price increase near the new airport compared with a distant control group.
- An Essendon study found a nonlinear property premium that peaked at 37% at 1.64 kilometers from the runway, while distance also served as a proxy for noise.
- A Southern California study of 23 airports found a greater price gradient under the flight paths of large airports than small airports.

These findings establish that property values are measurable socioeconomic outcomes, but they do not show the effect of a 500,000-passenger airport. They also illustrate why local impacts can be positive for accessibility and negative for amenity, depending on location and exposure.[Sustainability airport-property evidence table](https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/18/3/1580)

## 4. Causal attribution and counterfactual evidence

### Why airport impact totals are not automatically causal

Airport economic-impact studies commonly calculate the activity associated with airport operations and then apply input-output multipliers. They answer a contribution question: how much employment, income, output, or tax activity is linked to the airport’s measured operations under the model’s assumptions?

They do not necessarily answer the causal question: how much larger is the region because the airport exists or because passenger activity reached 500,000 rather than a lower level?

Several mechanisms can create a correlation without a causal airport effect:

- prosperous regions generate more air travel;
- airlines add routes where businesses and residents already create demand;
- public investment may expand both airports and surrounding economies;
- airport subsidies may maintain service in places with weak commercial demand;
- tourism, resource projects, universities, hospitals, or military activity may drive both traffic and employment;
- airport activity may divert passengers, cargo, or firms from another airport rather than create new regional activity; and
- the economic impact may occur outside the study region.

The FAA’s benefit-cost guidance explicitly warns that regional employment and other macroeconomic effects are difficult to quantify and may represent transfers from other regions. It requires a defined no-investment base case and incremental comparison of alternatives.[FAA airport benefit-cost guidance](https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/airports/central/airports_resources/1999_FAA_Airport_Benefit_Cost_Analysis_Guidance.pdf)

The FAA also cautions against treating employment or output multipliers as social benefits in public benefit-cost analyses without a separate counterfactual. This does not mean that airport employment or supplier spending is unreal; it means gross multiplier output is not automatically a net welfare gain.

### Evidence from quasi-experimental and panel designs

The strongest causal evidence in the supplied material is not tied to an airport exactly at 500,000 passengers, but it establishes that regional-airport activity can affect economic outcomes under some conditions.

Volkhausen uses the 1997 Single European Aviation market reform as a quasi-natural experiment. The study compares EU-15 NUTS-3 areas with regional airports with areas without them before and after the reform. It treats regions containing an airport or with a centroid within 25 kilometers as affected and excludes regions containing or adjacent to non-regional airports within a 20-kilometer buffer.

The study reports positive effects of regional-airport presence on economic activity of approximately 2–6%, population of 1–3%, and employment of about 2%. An instrumental-variable estimate reports a positive 2–3% GDP effect per additional 1 million passengers. The study defines regional airports as those below the European Commission’s 3-million-passenger ceiling and uses 2-million and 1-million thresholds as robustness checks.[Volkhausen regional-airport study](https://www.wiserpub.com/uploads/1/20220809/a34784bc2e82b267978ff56b9963ee42.pdf)

This is relevant but not directly transferable. The treatment category includes airports from zero up to 3 million passengers, the estimates are not centered on 500,000, and the policy reform changed the competitive and regulatory environment for a broad group of regions. The study also depends on assumptions about untreated regional trends and cannot eliminate every form of airport-location endogeneity.

The German evidence provides a counterexample. Breidenbach’s difference-in-differences analysis of the same reform found no evidence that regional-airport expansion generated regional growth in Germany, possibly because of limited statistical power. The contrast with the positive EU-15 result shows that regional-airport effects are heterogeneous rather than automatic.[Volkhausen review of German evidence](https://www.wiserpub.com/uploads/1/20220809/a34784bc2e82b267978ff56b9963ee42.pdf)

Fu and colleagues analyze all regions and 22 commercial airports in New Zealand from 2001 to 2016. Their fixed-effects, system-GMM, and dynamic common-correlated-effects models report that a 1% increase in total available seat kilometers is associated with a 0.38% increase in regional GDP per capita, holding other factors constant. The national coverage reduces concerns about traffic shifting among a selected group of airports, and the models address regional heterogeneity, cross-sectional dependence, and feedback effects.[Fu et al. airport-activity study](https://ira.lib.polyu.edu.hk/bitstream/10397/88971/1/Fu_Airport_Activities_Affect.pdf)

The New Zealand study includes scale points close to the threshold in scheduled seats: Nelson had 0.64 million scheduled seats in 2016 and Dunedin 0.60 million. These are seats, not passengers, and the study does not provide an exact 500,000-passenger result. It nevertheless supports the mechanism that the scale and quality of air service can affect regional GDP, especially where a region has one principal commercial airport and a clearly defined administrative catchment.

Bilotkach’s U.S. dynamic-panel GMM study similarly suggests that route structure and airline-market competition matter. Passenger volume affects employment and average wages but not business-establishment counts, while destination count is more robust. This weakens any claim that passenger throughput alone is a sufficient predictor of regional development.[Bilotkach airport-connectivity study](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0042098015576869)

A review of the wider literature reaches a mixed conclusion. Brueckner’s U.S. estimate associates a 10% increase in passenger enplanements with a 1% increase in service employment, with no particular manufacturing-employment effect. Sheard’s instrumental-variable studies find modest population and employment growth near airports, concentrated in services. Cidell finds that airport-centered job areas are only rarely the most important subregional job centers, while Mukkala and Tervo find clearer effects in peripheral than core regions.[Harvard CID synthesis of airport-development evidence](https://growthlab.hks.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/2020-06-cid-fellows-wp-127-albania-air-transport.pdf)

### Controlled before-and-after evidence outside the threshold cases

The property-market studies provide examples of counterfactual design. The Hong Kong airport-relocation study compares transactions near the new airport with transactions farther away before and after relocation and estimates a 24.43% relative price increase near the treatment airport. This is stronger than a simple airport-area correlation, but it identifies a relocation and accessibility shock, not the effect of 500,000 annual passengers on regional GDP or employment.[Sustainability airport-property evidence table](https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/18/3/1580)

The Norwegian research summarized by Future Transportation proposed a difference-in-differences input-output approach using regional-airport data from 1970 to 1980 while accounting for population growth and the development level of surrounding cities. The supplied material reports the design but not an effect size transferable to the threshold.[Future Transportation review](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-7590/3/3/62)

The Transportation Research Board’s case-study synthesis reaches a more cautious conclusion: in all but one airport region, origin-and-destination traffic and regional employment are highly correlated, but the direction of causation is unresolved. Growing employment may create more air traffic, more air traffic may create employment, or both may be driven by another factor.[TRB case-study synthesis](https://crp.trb.org/acrpwebresource12/measuring-air-service-and-regional-economic-activity/general-observations-of-the-case-studies/)

### Why the near-threshold cases do not identify a causal effect

The near-threshold cases provide useful exposure and outcome evidence but lack a common counterfactual.

**Prince George.** Passenger growth coincided with infrastructure investment, airport governance changes, route changes, resource-sector activity, and airline incentives. The airport transferred from federal government ownership to the Prince George Airport Authority in 2003, later expanded its terminal and runway, built a cargo warehouse, and used marketing and carrier incentives to support services such as Flair Airlines’ Tucson route. Its master plan explicitly states that air service decisions depend on airline business cases and that airport availability alone does not define the airport’s regional role.[YXS master plan](https://www.pgairport.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/PGAA_2023_Master_Plan_Update-Final_Report-2023_04_13_Compressed.pdf)

Prince George also experienced weaker demographic and labor-market growth than British Columbia between 2011 and 2021. The region’s population grew 6.2%, compared with 14% provincially; its workforce grew 2.4%, compared with 13%; and wage income increased 38%, compared with 45%. These trends are useful controls for context but are not an airport counterfactual.[Prince George economic profile](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/campaigns/immigration-matters/local-economies/prince-george.html)

**Newquay.** The airport’s 2021–2023 recovery followed COVID-19 closures and reopening, while the region’s tourism economy was also recovering. A before-and-after traffic increase cannot separate airport effects from the lifting of travel restrictions, new airlines, new destinations, and general tourism recovery.

**TRI.** The 2021–2023 traffic increase is similarly dominated by pandemic recovery. There is no matched comparison region or pre-trend test in the supplied material.

**Norwich and Newquay economic claims.** Both provide regional GVA claims near the threshold, but the supplied excerpts do not provide calculation models, comparison regions, traffic-year alignment, or uncertainty estimates. Their values establish that airport-linked regional effects are being measured, not that the airport caused the entire reported GVA.

**Hamilton.** The 2013 and 2017 impact studies do not form a clean before-and-after design. The 2017 estimate includes visitor expenditure effects that the 2013 estimate excludes, and the report uses different study methods. Cargo growth, e-commerce, industrial development, and airport investment also changed over the period.

**Gerald R. Ford International Airport.** Its 2023 study reports more than $500 million in Project Elevate infrastructure investment, 12 new nonstop routes since 2014, and pre-existing growth in Kent County and the wider region. The airport’s impact cannot be isolated from those investments and trends.[GFIA economic-impact study](https://www.grr.org/hubfs/GFIA%20Economic%20Impact%20Full%20Study%202023%20(002).pdf?hsLang=en)

**Norfolk.** ORF’s 2016–2019 comparison shows rising passengers, jobs, GDP, and output, but it has no control region and uses different IMPLAN versions. It demonstrates simultaneous growth, not a difference-in-differences effect.[Norfolk International Airport economic-impact study](http://www.flyorf.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/ORF-Economic-Impact-2019-FINAL-REPORT-22Jul2020.pdf)

### Displacement, leakage, and airport competition

A local airport may create new demand, retain spending that would otherwise leave the region, or merely shift traffic from another airport.

Hamilton provides an example of possible retention rather than wholly new demand. Its passenger service attracted travelers from southern Ontario who previously used airports near the U.S. border, including Buffalo Niagara. That may benefit Hamilton and retain local spending, but the net regional gain depends on the alternative airport, travel costs, and whether the spending would otherwise occur elsewhere.

Morimoto’s Japanese airport-choice study shows how route availability affects leakage. Passengers in Kitakyushu chose the local airport 79.3% of the time when it offered a direct connection to their destination, but only 0.9% when it did not. A one-minute reduction in access time increased local-airport choice probability by 1.1%, while one additional Tokyo flight increased it by 0.14%.[Morimoto airport-choice study](https://doi.org/10.20469/ijhss.5.10005-1)

These are airport-choice results rather than employment or GDP effects, but they demonstrate why a passenger count may reflect competition among airports rather than net new regional activity.

Leakage also differs by geographic boundary. Hamilton reports that roughly half of the airport-related impact leaks from Hamilton to the rest of Ontario. National models produce larger multipliers because the national economy retains more transactions. A local region may therefore receive a measurable direct benefit while capturing only a portion of the wider economic effect.

### Subsidies and public investment

Public support is not evidence against socioeconomic value, but it complicates net-benefit claims. Airports may be economically useful to residents and businesses while remaining financially dependent on operating aid or capital grants.

Prince George’s master plan identifies operating deficits of approximately $208,000 in 2023 and $82,000 in 2024 before projected operating surpluses from 2025 onward. It also identifies short-term annual funding requirements ranging from approximately $1.6 million to $14.2 million, or $2.1 million to $15 million when borrowing costs are included, depending on the timing of capital projects. The airport received $1.7 million in Airport Relief Fund support in 2022 and capital-assistance funding for equipment.[YXS master plan](https://www.pgairport.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/PGAA_2023_Master_Plan_Update-Final_Report-2023_04_13_Compressed.pdf)

ACIL Allen found that 22 of 36 Australian regional airports supplying financial data—61%—reported deficits in 2014/15. Excluding two airports with unusually large capital-works deficits, the reported deficits ranged from $10,300 to $3.26 million. This does not measure regional welfare, but it shows that local economic contribution and airport financial self-sufficiency are different outcomes.[ACIL Allen regional-airport analysis](https://treasury.gov.au/sites/default/files/2019-03/360985-Australian-Airports-Association-supporting-documents.pdf)

Oxera reports that five of six airports with fewer than 1 million passengers per annum in an earlier study were unlikely to become profitable by 2024. It also reports that many EU airports below 1 million passengers would continue to need operating aid, and that airports between 200,000 and 700,000 passengers could receive aid covering up to 80% of their operating funding gap under the 2014 state-aid framework.[Oxera regional-airport report](https://www.aci-europe.org/component/attachments/attachments.html?id=3123)

These findings refute the idea that 500,000 passengers is sufficient for financial independence. They do not refute the proposition that the airport can generate regional benefits. The relevant policy question is whether those benefits exceed the full opportunity cost of operating aid, capital investment, congestion, environmental effects, and alternative transport arrangements. The supplied near-threshold evidence does not establish that net balance.

## 5. Comparative magnitude and significance

### The best-aligned total-passenger calculation

The Canadian Airports Council reports that, on average, 1 million total passengers are associated with:

- 1,490 direct jobs;
- $116 million in direct wages;
- $174 million in direct GDP;
- $429 million in direct output; and
- $58 million in direct taxes.

A simple proportional translation to 500,000 total passengers is:

```math
\begin{aligned}&500{,}000 / 1{,}000{,}000 \times (1{,}490,\ \$116\text{m},\ \$174\text{m},\ \$429\text{m},\ \$58\text{m})\\&= (745,\ \$58\text{m},\ \$87\text{m},\ \$214.5\text{m},\ \$29\text{m})\end{aligned}
```

The calculation is useful because its exposure definition matches total passenger throughput. It should be read as a scale reference, not as a prediction for every airport. The underlying Canadian study draws on more than 30 airport studies, uses a 0.93 correlation between passenger volume and direct employment, estimates direct employment for 28 smaller airports through regression, and uses an input-output model for wages, GDP, output, and multiplier effects. It also acknowledges that there is no standardized airport-impact methodology.[Canadian Airports Council study](https://canadasairports.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/ACI-NA-Econ-Canada-Report-20250425.pdf)

The calculation has no supplied confidence interval. The 0.93 correlation is not a causal coefficient and does not express uncertainty around the 500,000 estimate. The figures also describe direct effects; they do not provide an airport-specific estimate of indirect, induced, or catalytic effects at the threshold.

### Alternative rates and why they cannot be combined as one range

Other sources provide materially different rates because they measure different exposures.

| Source and measure | Arithmetic at the relevant scale | What it measures | What it does not establish |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Canadian Airports Council, total passengers | 500,000 total passengers → approximately 745 direct jobs, $58m wages, $87m GDP, $214.5m output, and $29m taxes | Average direct airport-system contribution aligned with total passenger throughput | Exact airport effect, causation, confidence interval, local regional share, or net welfare |
| ACI-NA, additional enplanements | 500,000 additional enplanements → approximately 600 on-airport jobs and $193.6m on-airport output; visitor spending rises approximately $145.25m and supports 2,300 visitor jobs | Marginal U.S. estimate for additional boardings | Baseline effect of an airport with 500,000 total passengers or arrivals plus departures |
| Klophaus, additional passengers | 500,000 additional passengers → approximately 250 on-site jobs | On-site jobs at 17 German international airports | Visitor, supplier, induced, catalytic, or total regional effects |
| ACRP, departing seats | If 500,000 were departing seats, 0.005 jobs per seat at small hubs implies 2,500 jobs and 0.0114 at non-hubs implies 5,700 jobs | Association between departing seat capacity and regional employment | Total passenger throughput; unique passengers; causal jobs; applicability across airport types |

ACI-NA’s 2024 marginal rates are calculated from an average across U.S. commercial service airports. For every 1,000 additional enplanements, the study reports 1.2 additional on-airport jobs, $387,200 in on-airport output, $290,500 in visitor spending, and 4.6 visitor jobs. The 500,000 arithmetic is therefore:

```math
500{,}000 / 1{,}000 \times (1.2,\ \$387{,}200,\ 4.6,\ \$290{,}500) = (600,\ \$193.6\text{m},\ 2{,}300,\ \$145.25\text{m})
```

The on-airport and visitor quantities should not be collapsed into one output measure because one is output and the other is visitor spending. The combined job arithmetic would be approximately 2,900 jobs, but it remains a marginal additional-enplanement estimate, not a baseline estimate.[ACI-NA 2024 economic-impact study](https://airportscouncil.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/ACI-NA-The-Economic-Impact-of-U.S.-Commercial-Service-Airports-in-2024.pdf)

Klophaus’s German rule of thumb—500 on-site jobs per 1 million additional passengers—produces approximately 250 on-site jobs per 500,000 additional passengers. It is a useful comparison for direct airport employment but excludes regional visitor and multiplier effects.[Klophaus airport-employment study](https://doi.org/10.69554/ybxp3484)

ACRP’s departing-seat coefficients are more difficult to interpret for the hypothesis. They associate 0.005 regional jobs with each departing seat in small-hub areas and 0.0114 jobs per seat in non-hub areas. A departing seat is capacity, not a passenger movement, and the coefficients vary by airport type. They should not be used as a confidence interval around the Canadian total-passenger estimate.[ACRP Research Report 218 synthesis](https://crp.trb.org/acrpwebresource12/understanding-air-service-and-regional-economic-activity/the-role-of-aviation-in-supporting-local-economic-activity/)

The spread among these figures is not statistical uncertainty in the formal sense. It is evidence of measurement heterogeneity: total versus marginal exposure, passengers versus enplanements versus seats, on-site versus regional jobs, and different airport types.

### Absolute and relative significance

An effect of several hundred jobs or tens of millions of dollars can be practically significant in a small or peripheral region. It may be less significant in a metropolitan economy with hundreds of thousands of jobs and a diversified labor market.

Hamilton provides a direct relative comparison. Its 2017 study estimates that the airport supported about 3,450 jobs in the Hamilton region, while the region had more than 385,000 jobs. The airport’s total jobs therefore represented slightly less than 1% of regional employment, although its approximately 2,300 direct jobs placed it among the region’s ten largest employers. This is a meaningful local employer without being a dominant regional economic force.[Hamilton economic-impact analysis](https://flyhamilton.ca/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/HamiltonAirportEIAReport_FinalSubmitted.pdf)

Prince George is much smaller. The region’s 2021 profile reports 43,810 employed residents and $5.7 billion in household and business incomes. As noted earlier, applying the Canadian system-average scale mechanically would produce 745 direct jobs—about 1.7% of employed residents—and $87 million in GDP, approximately 1.5% of reported income. The calculation is illustrative rather than an airport estimate, but it shows how the same absolute effect can be more consequential in a smaller regional economy.

Norwich and Newquay report large GVA totals but do not provide the regional GDP or employment denominators needed to calculate shares. PSC reports modeled jobs, labor income, value added, and taxes but not Franklin County or its wider region’s employment and GDP denominator. TRI supplies connectivity and traffic but no regional outcome estimates. These missing denominators prevent a complete practical-significance ranking.

### Statistical significance and uncertainty

The supplied evidence does not provide a confidence interval for the effect of exactly 500,000 total annual passengers. Most near-threshold results are:

- airport-reported descriptive counts;
- sponsor-funded economic-impact claims;
- input-output model outputs;
- system-average regressions; or
- effects from different airport scales and exposure definitions.

GFIA’s visitor survey reports 1,516 completed surveys from 1,964 interview requests, a 77% response rate, a 95% confidence level, and a 5% margin of error. Those survey margins describe the visitor sample, not the uncertainty around the airport-wide jobs or output generated by the subsequent IMPLAN model.[GFIA economic-impact study](https://www.grr.org/hubfs/GFIA%20Economic%20Impact%20Full%20Study%202023%20(002).pdf?hsLang=en)

Fu and colleagues report significant regional-economic effects across their New Zealand panel models, but the supplied material does not provide a threshold-specific confidence interval. Volkhausen reports positive estimates from quasi-experimental and instrumental-variable models, but the supplied evidence does not provide a transferable confidence interval for 500,000 passengers. The absence of an interval is a limitation, not evidence that the effect is zero.

### Costs, subsidies, and net regional welfare

Gross economic activity cannot be compared directly with airport capital costs unless the units, time horizon, geography, and counterfactual are aligned.

Prince George’s master plan identifies approximately $64.8 million of short-term capital projects for 2024–2028, along with additional medium- and long-term rehabilitation and development. Its financial outlook says that projected operating surpluses are insufficient to cover all short-term capital expenses and that external funding may be needed. The airport can therefore support regional services and jobs while still requiring public capital support.

The Australian below-500,000 evidence similarly shows a distinction between regional impact and airport financial performance. Operator expenditure and induced spending are measurable, while 61% of surveyed airports reported operating deficits. Oxera’s evidence that many sub-million-passenger European airports require operating aid reinforces the same point. Financial viability is not a substitute for regional welfare, but it is essential to a public investment decision.

The FAA’s benefit-cost guidance recommends a no-investment base case, reasonable alternatives, an evaluation period, and explicit uncertainty. A threshold-specific net-benefit claim would need to account for:

- airport operating aid;
- capital rehabilitation and expansion;
- airline incentives and marketing support;
- road, rail, and public-transit investments;
- passenger and cargo diversion from other airports;
- imported inputs and regional leakage;
- congestion, noise, and property effects;
- environmental costs; and
- the value of connectivity and avoided travel costs.

No supplied near-threshold study combines these elements into a net regional welfare estimate.

## 6. Evidence quality, limitations, and heterogeneity

### Exposure definitions are not standardized

The central limitation is that the cases do not measure the same thing.

YXS’s 2018 profile explicitly includes arrivals, departures, and connections. Its master plan uses enplaned/deplaned passengers. Newquay and TRI use “PAX” or “total passengers” without defining the directional basis. PSC reports scheduled enplanements. Hamilton reports passengers alongside large cargo volumes. ACI-NA’s marginal estimate uses additional enplanements, while Klophaus uses additional passengers and ACRP uses departing seats.

These measures answer different questions. A total-passenger series is appropriate for baseline airport scale; enplanements are useful for airport classification and marginal boarding effects; departing seats measure available capacity; and passenger-choice studies measure demand leakage. They cannot be pooled without assumptions that the supplied evidence does not support.

### Traffic and outcome years are poorly aligned

YXS has a 2018 near-threshold traffic profile but a 2011 employment and wage estimate. Norwich’s traffic count is for the year ending March 2026, while the supplied GVA assessment has no disclosed study year. Newquay’s traffic and GVA claims appear in the 2024/25 sustainability report, but the calculation period is not fully described. Hamilton’s 2017 traffic and impact data are aligned more closely, but cargo dominates the result and the comparison with 2013 is not like-for-like.

The pandemic creates an additional break. U.S. enplanements fell from 902.7 million in 2019 to 365.3 million in 2020, a 59.5% decline. Canadian passenger traffic fell from 162.9 million to 46.3 million, a 71.5% decline. Newquay closed and reopened; YXS traffic fell 64%; TRI’s 2021–2023 increase reflects recovery. A post-2020 rise cannot be interpreted as a long-run airport treatment effect without accounting for restrictions, reopening, labor shortages, route restoration, and macroeconomic recovery.[ACI-NA 2024 study](https://airportscouncil.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/ACI-NA-The-Economic-Impact-of-U.S.-Commercial-Service-Airports-in-2024.pdf)[Canadian Airports Council study](https://canadasairports.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/ACI-NA-Econ-Canada-Report-20250425.pdf)

### Geographic boundaries alter the result

Direct airport employment is usually concentrated on the airport site. Indirect and induced effects depend on where workers live, where suppliers operate, and how much spending remains within the study boundary. Visitor spending depends on where passengers stay and consume services.

The Hamilton study shows approximately half of the total effect outside Hamilton. The Palomar study finds that North County accounts for 63% of regional employment impact and 52% of industry activity, while Carlsbad alone accounts for 35% of employment impact and 36% of activity. The DCRA study includes eight counties; GFIA includes Kent County and a 13-county region; ORF reports Commonwealth-wide totals while describing a metropolitan area; and YXS is discussed variously as serving Prince George, the Regional District of Fraser-Fort George, and Northern British Columbia.

A result measured over a wide region may be useful for regional planning but cannot be compared directly with an airport-local result. Wider geography can increase measured multiplier effects through reduced leakage while also diluting the airport’s share of regional employment and GDP.

### Input-output models measure modeled contribution, not necessarily net causation

IMPLAN and similar models are useful for translating direct airport activity into supplier and household-spending effects. They generally assume fixed production relationships, use local-purchase coefficients, and do not automatically identify what would have happened without the airport.

The Canadian study states that there is no standardized airport-impact methodology. It combines more than 30 airport studies with different definitions and uses regression for smaller airports. ACI-NA similarly combines statewide and individual airport studies and estimates missing data through regression before applying national IMPLAN multipliers.

The models can also omit or misstate:

- displacement from other airports or transport modes;
- jobs filled by workers who would otherwise work elsewhere;
- visitors who would have traveled to the region by road or another airport;
- imports and purchases outside the region;
- the difference between temporary construction jobs and permanent jobs;
- environmental and congestion costs; and
- the distribution of benefits among residents, firms, and governments.

The Crete airport study makes similar warnings: input-output results are static, peak-year studies may overstate effects, recession-year studies may understate them, and imported intermediate inputs create leakage. The FAA likewise cautions that multiplier-generated output may represent transfers rather than net social gains.

### Sponsor funding and internal inconsistencies

Airport economic-impact studies are often commissioned or funded by airport authorities, airport sponsors, industry groups, or public agencies. That does not make their results unusable, but it increases the importance of transparent methods and independent validation.

The Norwich announcement describes its assessment as independent but does not provide the underlying report in the supplied material. Newquay’s GVA and social-value claims appear in an airport sustainability report, and the social-value figure is explicitly subject to verification. Hamilton’s ICF report was commissioned for the airport. GFIA’s report was funded by the Gerald R. Ford International Airport Authority. ACI-NA and the Canadian Airports Council use broad multi-airport models but acknowledge methodological variation.

Several supplied reports also contain internal numerical inconsistencies:

- Hamilton’s executive summary gives one set of cargo employment, labor-income, and activity figures, while its detailed table gives another.
- ORF reports 4,864,752 total 2024 passengers in its passenger-activity table but 4,862,000 in its scheduled-landings table.
- GFIA’s summary reports 30,883 Kent County jobs, while a detailed table prints 27,025; the listed components sum to approximately 30,882.
- DCRA reports $2,573.8 million in one total-sales table and $2,530.2 million in another without reconciling the difference.
- YXS’s official sources report different 2019 traffic figures and use different passenger definitions.

These inconsistencies do not prove that the reported impacts are false. They do mean that the figures should be treated as estimates with reporting caveats, not as exact measurements.

### The outcome evidence is uneven

| Outcome | Evidence near the threshold | Evidence gap |
|---|---|---|
| Airport employment | YXS reports 770 person-years in 2011; Norwich reports about 250 direct employees; PSC models 1,467 direct jobs and 2,194 total jobs; the Canadian model supplies a 745-job direct proxy for 500,000 total passengers. | No same-year, standardized direct-employment series for an airport at exactly 500,000 total passengers. |
| Regional employment and unemployment | Norwich reports 2,840 jobs; Newquay reports GVA but not jobs; PSC reports statewide modeled jobs; regional profiles provide denominators without airport attribution. | No near-threshold matched control, unemployment estimate, or regional employment share with causal identification. |
| Wages and household income | YXS reports $24 million wages; PSC reports $99.128 million labor income; the Canadian direct proxy is $58 million wages; larger studies report wages and compensation. | No threshold-specific causal household-income effect and no consistent treatment of FTEs, benefits, or proprietor income. |
| GDP, GVA, and output | Norwich reports £184 million GVA; Newquay approximately £100 million GVA; PSC $173.516 million value added; Canadian proxy $87 million direct GDP and $214.5 million output. | Methods, denominators, currencies, and geographic boundaries differ; no common regional GDP share. |
| Business activity and investment | YXS identifies resource, logistics, and airport-land opportunities; Hamilton documents cargo and MRO; broader studies link routes to business formation and investment. | No near-threshold causal estimate of business formation, productivity, or investment. |
| Tourism and visitor spending | Newquay and Norwich identify tourism or business connectivity; larger ORF and DCRA studies quantify visitor spending. | No standardized near-threshold visitor count, spending estimate, or inbound-versus-outbound decomposition. |
| Tax revenue | PSC reports $11.628 million modeled taxes; the Canadian proxy is $29 million direct taxes; larger ORF and DCRA cases report much larger totals. | No threshold-specific net fiscal balance after airport expenditure and public aid. |
| Property values | Non-threshold studies show positive, negative, and nonlinear effects depending on noise, access, and relocation. | No property-value study linked to an airport near 500,000 passengers. |
| Connectivity and productivity | Norwich, TRI, and YXS report route networks; Bilotkach and Fu provide broader empirical support for connectivity and aviation activity. | No quantified productivity or GDP effect for exactly 500,000 total passenger movements. |
| Statistical uncertainty | Some broader studies use DiD, IV, GMM, or panel estimators; GFIA reports survey confidence parameters. | No confidence interval or p-value for a 500,000-total-passenger airport effect. |
| Net regional welfare | FAA guidance and airport financial studies identify the need to account for costs, transfers, and leakage. | No near-threshold audit combines benefits, subsidies, capital costs, displacement, and environmental effects. |

### Heterogeneity is substantive, not statistical noise

The cases differ in ways that can change the effect per passenger.

Norwich connects a regional economy to offshore energy and a large international network through Amsterdam. Newquay is strongly tied to tourism and local suppliers. YXS serves a geographically dispersed, resource-oriented region and supports medical, wildfire, cargo, and charter activities. TRI connects a four-state catchment to five hubs. PSC combines passenger service with cargo, general aviation, agriculture, flight training, and emergency operations. Hamilton’s result is dominated by express cargo and logistics.

These airports can have similar passenger totals while supporting very different labor markets and output. Passenger volume is therefore a useful scale indicator but not a sufficient statistic for socioeconomic impact.

The literature also suggests that peripheral regions may benefit more than already well-connected core regions. A local airport can reduce travel time, improve access to specialized workers, and retain spending that would otherwise leave the area. In a large, well-connected metropolitan region, the same passenger increment may produce a smaller relative effect because existing alternatives are abundant and the regional economy is less dependent on one airport.

## 7. Overall support, refutation, or conditional verdict

### Finding by outcome

The evidence supports the following judgments:

| Outcome | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Direct airport employment and wages | Supported as measurable. Near-threshold cases report direct jobs, person-years, labor income, or wages, although definitions differ. |
| Regional employment and GVA/GDP | Conditionally supported. Norwich, Newquay, PSC, and larger comparators report substantial regional measures, but the closest cases lack transparent causal designs. |
| Indirect and induced activity | Supported as modeled activity. Supplier purchases and worker re-spending are measurable in IMPLAN and similar models, but gross multipliers are not automatically net regional gains. |
| Tourism and visitor spending | Supported where the airport brings non-local visitors and the region can absorb their spending. The effect is weaker when passengers are local residents or traffic is diverted from another airport. |
| Connectivity and productivity | Supported as a plausible and increasingly well-evidenced mechanism. Route diversity, destination count, competition, cargo, and business travel appear important, but no exact 500,000-passenger productivity estimate is available. |
| Tax revenue | Supported as gross measurable revenue. Net fiscal benefit remains unestablished because public operating and capital costs are not consistently included. |
| Property values | Airport effects can be positive or negative locally, but no near-threshold property estimate is available. |
| Statistical significance at exactly 500,000 total passengers | Not established. The supplied evidence contains no exact threshold study with a reported confidence interval and control-region design. |
| Universal or automatic significance | Not supported. The German null result, modest airport-area findings, financial deficits, leakage, and route-mix differences all contradict a one-size-fits-all threshold. |

### What the evidence supports

The strongest support comes from the convergence of several kinds of evidence.

First, airports close to the threshold report measurable outcomes. Norwich reports approximately £184 million in GVA and 2,840 jobs at 453,000 passengers. Newquay reports approximately £100 million in regional GVA at 400,311 reported PAX. YXS reports 770 person-years and $24 million in wages in an earlier period and documents a broad airport ecosystem at roughly the requested traffic scale. PSC reports 2,194 modeled jobs, $173.516 million in value added, and $11.628 million in taxes at 395,348 scheduled enplanements.

Second, the total-passenger Canadian model produces a coherent scale estimate for 500,000 passengers: approximately 745 direct jobs, $58 million in direct wages, $87 million in direct GDP, $214.5 million in direct output, and $29 million in direct taxes. The estimate is not causal, but it demonstrates that a half-million-passenger airport can be associated with outcomes large enough to appear in regional economic accounts.

Third, broader causal and quasi-causal studies find positive effects of airport presence, available seat capacity, connectivity, and destination count on regional employment, wages, business establishments, or GDP in at least some settings. Volkhausen’s European reform design, Fu’s New Zealand panel, Bilotkach’s U.S. connectivity model, and the property-market difference-in-differences evidence all support the proposition that airport-related access can affect regional outcomes beyond the airport boundary.

### What the evidence does not support

The evidence does not support treating 500,000 as a natural economic breakpoint. No supplied study shows that an airport below 500,000 has negligible effects and an airport above 500,000 suddenly produces large effects. The European policy thresholds of 200,000, 700,000, 1 million, and 3 million passengers relate to aid eligibility or airport classification, not a demonstrated socioeconomic discontinuity.[Oxera regional-airport report](https://www.aci-europe.org/component/attachments/attachments.html?id=3123)[Volkhausen regional-airport study](https://www.wiserpub.com/uploads/1/20220809/a34784bc2e82b267978ff56b9963ee42.pdf)

The evidence also does not support attributing all reported regional activity to passenger throughput. In several cases, cargo, resource-sector travel, tourism, infrastructure investment, emergency services, or airport-land development may be more important than scheduled passengers. YXS’s own master plan states that the airport facilitates demand generated by regional businesses rather than creating all of that demand itself. Hamilton’s results show how cargo can dominate a near-threshold passenger case.

Nor does the evidence establish a net regional benefit after costs. Airports below this scale can require operating aid and substantial capital funding. An airport may generate regional jobs and visitor spending while imposing public funding requirements or transferring activity from other regions. A gross impact estimate is not a cost-benefit result.

### Final verdict

The hypothesis is **conditionally supported**.

An airport handling approximately 500,000 annual passenger movements can generate significant and measurable socioeconomic effects in its surrounding region. The supported effects include direct airport employment, supplier and induced activity, wages, output, GVA or GDP, visitor spending, tax revenue, and improved connectivity. The Canadian system estimate provides a plausible total-passenger scale reference, while Norwich, Newquay, YXS, and PSC demonstrate that near-threshold airports can have visible regional economic footprints.

The effect is more likely to be practically significant when the airport provides scarce connectivity, serves a large or remote catchment, supports tourism or business travel, handles cargo, connects resource industries, retains spending that would otherwise leave the region, and operates within a regional economy capable of absorbing additional activity. It is likely to be smaller, more redistributive, or more subsidy-dependent when traffic is weakly connected, primarily outbound, highly seasonal, diverted from another airport, or accompanied by substantial leakage and fixed costs.

Thus, 500,000 passengers is a credible scale at which regional impacts can be measured, but it is not a guarantee of a large causal or net socioeconomic effect. The strongest defensible conclusion is not “500,000 passengers always matters” or “500,000 passengers is too few to matter,” but rather: **the threshold can matter substantially in the right airport and regional context, and the context—not the passenger count alone—determines the magnitude and welfare significance.**
